tip: 'Vouloir dire' literally reads 'to want to say', but together it just means 'to mean': 'qu'est-ce que ça veut dire' = what does that mean?
In everyday French, 'on' means 'we': 'où est-ce qu'on se retrouve' = where do we meet? It takes a singular verb even though it means us.
A day 'passes itself' in French: 'comment s'est passée ta journée'. 'Se passer' means to happen, and it takes 'être' in the past.
'Ne...jamais de' = never any. Same rule: 'un/une/du/de la' become 'de' in the negative: 'je ne bois jamais de café'.
French often builds adverbs like English '-ly': '-ment' on the feminine adjective, so 'lente' (slow) gives 'lentement' (slowly) – 'plus lentement' = more slowly.
French can't strand a preposition at the end: it's 'pour qui est ce cadeau', literally 'for whom is this gift', never a dangling 'for'.
Languages normally take 'le' in French: you don't learn 'French', you learn 'le français' – hence 'apprends le français'.
'Il y a' covers both 'there is' and 'there are' – it never changes for number: 'il y a trop de bruit', 'il y a trois livres'.
'Du' = 'de' + 'le', and 'des' = 'de' + 'les'. These contractions are mandatory: 'le livre du professeur', 'les jouets des enfants'.
'Ne...plus de' = no more. Like 'ne...pas de', the article disappears after the negative + 'de': 'il n'y a plus de pain'.
'Être en train de' + verb = to be in the middle of doing something. Use it to emphasize an ongoing action: 'je suis en train de travailler'.
'Aimer' takes 'le/la/les' for general likes: 'tu aimes le fromage' asks about cheese in general, not one specific cheese.
'Entrée' here means the entrance. On a menu it's the starter course, never the main dish – English borrowed the word and flipped its meaning.
Flip verb and subject for a polite question: 'voulez-vous...?' = do you want. The hyphen links them – 'vous voulez' becomes 'voulez-vous'.
'Mon/ma/mes' match the noun that follows, not the owner: 'mon père' (m.), 'ma mère' (f.), 'mes parents' (pl.).
'Son/sa/ses' = his/her/its. The form matches the following noun's gender, not the owner: 'son mari' = her husband.
'Au' = 'à' + 'le', 'aux' = 'à' + 'les' – mandatory: 'je vais au marché', 'je parle aux enfants'. No contraction with 'la' or 'l''.
'Souvenir' means a memory first, a keepsake second – both from the verb 'se souvenir' (to remember). So 'des souvenirs' can be either.
Nationality adjectives in '-ien' change to '-ienne' for the feminine: 'italien' becomes 'italienne'. Same with 'canadien'/'canadienne'.
'Des' is the plural of 'un/une': 'des frites' = some fries. French requires it where English often says nothing.
'Depuis quand' = since when; 'depuis combien de temps' = for how long. Both normally take the present tense in French, not the past.
After quantity words like 'beaucoup de', 'peu de', 'trop de', 'assez de', use 'de' without an article: 'beaucoup de pain', not 'du pain'.
'Il te reste du temps' is literally 'there remains time to you': French uses 'rester' (to remain) where English says 'have...left'.
'Du fromage' (some cheese) and 'de la confiture' (some jam) – 'du' and 'de la' mark an unspecified amount.
'Laisser' plus an adjective means to leave something in a state: 'a laissé la fenêtre ouverte' = left the window open. 'Ouverte' agrees with 'fenêtre'.
Adjectives ending in '-eux' swap to '-euse' in the feminine: 'courageux' becomes 'courageuse'. Same with 'heureux/heureuse', 'sérieux/sérieuse'.
'Il faut' isn't 'he must' – it means 'it takes' or 'one needs': 'il faut du courage' = courage is needed. The 'il' is a dummy subject, like English 'it' in 'it rains'.
'Beau' becomes 'bel' before a vowel sound: 'un beau pays' but 'un bel été'. 'Vieux' does the same: 'vieil homme'.
After a quantity word, French drops the article: 'un morceau de gâteau', never 'de la'. Same for 'un kilo de', 'une tasse de'.
A few adjectives sit before the noun, and you can stack them: 'un joli petit village' puts both 'joli' and 'petit' up front, unlike most French adjectives.
